title: Positioning statements and communicating positioning
summary: A positioning statement names the target customers and the key benefit. Positioning is communicated through category, parity, difference and story.

chunks.heading: Crafting a positioning statement
chunks.explanation_md:
A **positioning statement** articulates the **target customers** and the **key benefit**.

Example: for convenience minded pizza lovers (target customers), Domino's offers a hot delicious pizza, delivered promptly to your door (value proposition). Describe attributes versus the benefits those attributes deliver.

When **communicating** the positioning, the statement conveys the offering's **category membership** with **points of parity and points of difference**, and develops a **narrative**. Example: for health-conscious young professionals, Brand X is a convenient healthy meal solution that provides nutritious food without compromising taste because it uses fresh, locally sourced ingredients.

chunks.heading: Conflicting benefits and positioning as storytelling
chunks.explanation_md:
**Communicating conflicting benefits.** The challenge: consumers want to maximize both of two **negatively correlated** attributes or benefits. Two responses: **develop a product or service that performs well on both dimensions**, or **launch different marketing campaigns**.

**Positioning as storytelling.** Consumers rarely think in terms of frames of reference or points of difference: **they think in stories**. The slide shows a dusty vehicle overloaded with many men, with FEVICOL printed on its side.

questions.stem: Explain how a firm crafts and communicates a positioning statement, including how it deals with conflicting benefits.
questions.model_answer_md:
A **positioning statement** articulates the target customers and the key benefit. In the example, Domino's offers convenience minded pizza lovers a hot delicious pizza delivered promptly to the door. The statement should say what the attributes deliver as benefits.

To **communicate** the positioning, the firm conveys category membership along with points of parity and points of difference and develops a narrative, as in the Brand X statement for health-conscious young professionals.

When consumers want two **negatively correlated** benefits at once, the firm can develop a product that performs well on both dimensions or launch different marketing campaigns.

Consumers rarely think in frames of reference or points of difference; they think in stories.

**Conclusion.** A good positioning statement is then told as a story.
